item.title: Artspace Guåhan to open ‘You Are Here’ exhibition
item.description: Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning. The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.
item.content:encoded:
Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning.

The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.

The exhibition centers on the question, “What does HERE mean to YOU?” and invites visitors to consider their own connections to place and belonging through the artwork on display.

Artspace Guåhan will bring together artists with different perspectives and ask visitors to consider what being “ here ” means to them. Deane Jessee-Jones, secretary of the board of directors, says the exhibition supports local artists of varying ages.

She said, “We do not collect any commission… all of the profits go directly to the artist.”

Artspace Guåhan is a Guam-based nonprofit that works to make art accessible and provide opportunities for local artists to exhibit and connect with the community.

The opening runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. and will include an opportunity to meet the artists.

The exhibition will remain on display through Dec. 3.

You Are Here is free and open to the public.

item.title: U.S. Supreme Court hears arguments in Andersen open detonation case
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base. The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base.

The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.

In May 2021, the Air Force applied for a three-year renewal of its hazardous waste facility permit with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency. In court filings, Prutehi Guåhan stated that the Air Force failed to conduct an environmental assessment of its actions as required by the National Environmental Policy Act.

The case was dismissed in the District Court of Guam, but the 9 th Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Prutehi Guåhan and reinstated the case.

The Supreme Court is considering whether the Air Force’s request to renew its permit would be a “final agency action” that can be reviewed by the courts. Justices are also considering whether federal agencies must comply with NEPA requirements before seeking to renew environmental permits.

During oral arguments before the court, Department of Justice attorney Sopan Joshi argued that filing a permit application is not a final agency action.

“It’s a request to someone else to take action,” he said. “Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee, asked Joshi when the Air Force’s decision to operate the detonation pit would be considered final.

“So are you saying that there’s no point at which the Air Force’s decision can be challenged?” he asked. “The Air Force’s action is never final and, therefore, never reviewable?”

“The application is never going to become final agency action,” Joshi said. “And there is no cause of action under NEPA itself. Congress didn't provide one. So any review would have to go through the [Administrative Procedure Act], and I don't think the APA provides a cause of action for this application at any point in time.”

Earthjustice attorney Caroline Flynn, representing Prutehi Guåhan, said the Air Force’s final action is clear.

“We know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.”

The justices will consider the arguments, and a ruling will likely take several months.

item.title: ‘Struggling to keep this government going’: Apatang warns of furloughs, rising austerity after signing strained CNMI budget
item.description: The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues. Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.
item.content:encoded:
The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues.

Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.

Apatang said he vetoed several provisions he deemed unconstitutional or financially impossible, including a mandate requiring the administration to “front‑load” $16 million to the Public School System. He said the CNMI cannot afford the upfront payment and must instead fund PSS monthly. The Senate’s final budget version allocates $25 million for PSS—down from the $32 million proposed by both the governor and the House.

“It breaks my heart to reduce PSS funding,” Apatang said, adding that a three‑day school week would be unacceptable but may be unavoidable unless the PSS board finds operational efficiencies.

The governor said the administration is “scraping the bottom of the barrel,” warning that furloughs—estimated at up to 400 employees—may be necessary once Civil Service Commission regulations are finalized. He also confirmed retirees will lose their 25% government contribution after Oct. 15, though he is searching for funds to soften the impact.

Apatang defended his administration against criticism over the CNMI’s fiscal collapse, saying he inherited years of unresolved audit findings and depleted federal relief funds.

“I didn’t spend all this money,” he said. “We’re struggling to keep this government going.”

He urged agencies to tighten operations, reduce expenses, and avoid unnecessary vehicle use. He also asked Commonwealth Public Utilities Corp. to reconsider CUC’s proposed rate increase, calling it “a drastic burden” residents cannot afford.

On tourism and economic recovery, Apatang said federal immigration and travel policies continue to hinder the CNMI’s ability to rebuild air service and visitor arrivals. He said he has repeatedly asked federal officials to visit the Commonwealth and understand its strategic importance.

With three months left in his term, Apatang said the next administration will face a difficult road.

“Good luck,” he said. “I’ll pray for you. It’s going to be a tough one.”

item.title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego
item.description: The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew. item.content:encoded:
The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

Hegseth told the crew that President Donald Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."

The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.

The Navy initially downplayed any problems, and Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."

The carrier had left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.

Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

item.title: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
item.description: NEW YORK — U.S. authorities charged former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with conspiring to torture his fellow citizens in order to maintain his hold on power. item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — U.S. authorities charged former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with conspiring to torture his fellow citizens in order to maintain his hold on power. The new indictment, unsealed Thursday, adds pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking offenses.

Maduro, who was previously charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., is now also facing allegations of human rights abuses during his reign as president of the oil-rich South American nation.

"He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," says the revised indictment, which newly charges Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, with torture conspiracy.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.

Asserting that thousands of Venezuelans were "harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed" by people acting at the behest of the government that Maduro controlled, the indictment alleges that the abuse included electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on methods of torture and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."

A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer; Flores was in court for a previously scheduled hearing, where her attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations. Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.

Both have pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They had already been facing potential life prison sentences if convicted.

Maduro has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.

The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York, and has offered to testify against his former boss.

The indictment alleges that the torture victims included three U.S. citizens, who were not named in the court documents.

One of those Americans was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.

Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.

Flores, meanwhile, was in court Thursday so her lawyers could urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.

Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.

Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail, and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.

They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.

Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.

Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public" if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital, when care was needed.

President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.

Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is "intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence."

item.title: 4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
item.description: Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station. The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles
item.content:encoded:
Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station.

The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., on Thursday, aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.

Their trip home started about 45 minutes before, at an orbital speed of 17,500 mph.

The spacecraft lit its thrusters to nudge it out of orbit, causing the capsule to plunge into the atmosphere, its ablative heat shield battling extreme temperatures (up to 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit) during the fiery reentry. Over the course of about half an hour, the capsule slowed to a few hundred miles per hour, and then four orange-and-white parachutes took over, easing the spacecraft to just 16 mph above the cool, blue ocean and a gentle plop into the water.

The Crew-12 mission was the 20th time SpaceX had sent humans into orbit, lifting off in February on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. It docked with the space station the next day . During the eight months in space, NASA said the crew completed dozens of science experiments and research, including studies of stem cells, how crystals grow in space and bone loss in microgravity.

Not all of their work happened inside the space station. Meir conducted four spacewalks totaling just over 27 hours to perform maintenance and upgrade the aging orbital outpost. Adenot performed three spacewalks.

Before departing, members of the Crew-12 mission were relieved by the three astronauts and cosmonaut of Crew-13 , who arrived at the space station last week to start a six-month rotation.

During a pre-departure news conference on the station last month, Meir said she couldn't wait to be reunited with her 3 1/2-year-old daughter.

But there was something else she missed after all this time in orbit. "So looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves. Experiencing all those things that we don't have up here," she said.

The two-time space veteran said there were two things she'd miss about space: weightlessness and the wonderful views of Earth.

item.title: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
item.description: SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine ref
item.content:encoded:
SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.

North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.

It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.

Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.

South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,
